full_judgment:
The present petitioner Meher Negar on 6.10.86 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 42 of 1986 in the Court of erstwhile Upazila Magistrate. Kalkini in the District of Madaripur, under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against her husband, the opposite party before us, namely, Md. Mojibur Rahman, claiming maintenance for herself and her son aged about 15 months, alleging that the opposite party in spite of having capacity was not maintaining her and the minor son after driving them out from his house on 26.9.85. It was further stated in the petition that as per condition laid down in the registered Kabinnama of the marriage between the parties the opposite party was bound to pay Taka 300.00 for the child. The Magistrate issued processes upon the opposite party who did not appear and so the learned Magistrate after hearing the petitioner ordered for payment of Taka 300.00 and Taka 200.00 per month for the maintenance of the petitioner wife and the child respectively, vide order dated 20.12.86, Thereafter the opposite party husband preferred Criminal Motion No. 13 of 1987 before the Sessions Judge. Madaripur who in his impugned judgment and order dated 16.3.87 came to the finding that with the coming into force of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. XVIII of 1985) with effect from 15th June, 1985, Magistrates were divested of the powers under section 488 CrPC to puss any order for maintenance as because the jurisdiction to entertain and dispose of a prayer for maintenance vested exclusively in the Family Court constituted under the Ordinance and, as such, the impugned order of the Magistrate granting maintenance to the wife and son under section 488 CrPC being passed after coming into force of the Ordinance, was without jurisdiction and of no legal effect. Accordingly, the learned Sessions Judge allowed the motion and set aside the order of the learned Magistrate directing payment of maintenance. Being aggrieved the original petitioner of the Miscellaneous Case has come tip with this revisional application under section 439 CrPC and has obtained the Rule. 

 10. In section 5 of the Ordinance of 1985 it has been provided that a Family Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of any suit relating to or arising out of any matters enumerated in clauses (a) to (e) of that section. We have underlined the words "any suit" appearing in this section as we want to put emphasis on these two words. If the provisions of section 5 are examined carefully then it will become crystal clear that the Family Court has been empowered to entertain, try and dispose of suits relating to or arising out of the 5 matters including maintenance mentioned in the section itself. Moreover, section 6 of the Ordinance lays down the procedure to be followed in filing a suit before the Family Court and it also includes the provision for returning the plaint for presentation in the Court to which it should have been presented. Section 22 provides for payment of fixed court fee of Taka 25.00. Section 16 provides procedure for enforcement of decree passed by a Family Court. From the above provisions of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 it becomes crystal clear that the proceedings before the Family Court shall be absolutely civil in nature and a decree passed by such Court shall be treated as a civil decree passed in a money suit or in any other class suit. On the other hand, under no stretch of imagination it can be said that section 488 CrPC empowers a Magistrate to entertain a plaint or to dispose of any matter which is civil in nature. A Magistrate can entertain only a petition by the aggrieved party and dispose of the matter in a summary manner and such a proceeding before a Magistrate can rightly be termed as a quasi-criminal and quasi-judicial proceeding. On the other hand, section 5 of the Ordinance of 1985 empowers the Family Courts with exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of suits relating to any matter enumerated in that section. In the case of Abdul Khaleque (Md) Vs. Selina Begum and another, reported in 42 DLR 450, a Single Judge of the High Court Division has held: 

 "There will be anomaly and multiplicity of proceeding and practical difficulties will arise, if, in spite of the establishment of the Family Courts by Ordinance No. XVIII of 1985, the Magistrate continued to entertain cases for maintenance under section 488 CrPC. Section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance gives exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of any suit relating to or arising out of all or any of the family matters including maintenance. To my mind, this provision along with sections 3 and 23 seems to have ousted the jurisdiction of the Magistrates to entertain application under section 488, CrPC and to grant maintenance which is a Family Courts matter now." 

 11. In this judgment the learned Single Judge has taken into consideration the provisions of section 5 of the West Pakistan Family Court Act. 1964 and section 5 of Ordinance No XVIII of 1985 which is our law. The learned Judge in doing so has pointed out certain distinctions in the language used in the two legislations including the use of the word 'suit' in our law and the word 'matters' appearing in section 5 of the West Pakistan Act and has observed that by suits it is generally understood that matters of civil nature and has also pointed out that a proceeding under section 488 is of quasi criminal and quasi-civil nature. The learned Judge also took into notice the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in PLD 1969 (SC) 187 and Supreme Court Monthly Review (Vol. IV) of 1971, 150. But the learned Judge in coming to the finding that the provisions of sections 3, 5 and 27 of the Ordinance of 1985 have ousted the jurisdiction of the Magistrate to entertain a petition for maintenance under section 488CrPC has not tried to explain as to how the term 'suit' which is a term of the civil law can include a miscellaneous petition in a quasi-criminal and quasi-judicial proceeding under section 488 CrPC. Moreover, it appears that the learned Judge relied on the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in PLD 1969 (SC) 187, but it escaped his notice that in that judgment Me Justice Hamoodur Rahman, the Chief Justice of Pakistan, has specifically mentioned section 20 of the West Pakistan Family Court Act, 1964 which empowers the Government to invest any judge of the Family Court with the powers of Magistrate, 1st Class to make order for maintenance under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,1898 and in exercise of that power all Judges of the Family Court were invested with the powers of the Magistrate, 1st Class to make order for maintenance under section 488 CrPC by notification issued on 5th April, 1966. Thus we find that the West Pakistan Law contains a provision for vesting the power under section 488 to the Judges of the Family Court and accordingly, the Government invested those judges with that power as early as in 1966 and in view of the above legal position the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that after that investment of power to the judges or the Family Court the Magistrate ceased to have power to order for maintenance under section 488 CrPC. 

 15. The order of the Sessions Judge, Madaripur passed in Criminal Motion No. 13 of 1987 is hereby set aside and that of the Magistrate, Kalkini passed in Miscellaneous Cass No. 42 of 1986 is restored.
